citation: eCFR. 13 CFR 121.103 How does SBA determine affiliation?. 2026-10-01. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-121/subpart-A/subject-group-ECFRd133f03f6d8398b/section-121.103

date_note: Sweep gave published: up to date as of 10/01/2026; section last amended 1/16/2025 per the eCFR timeline
summary: The affiliation rule. Paragraph (h) defines a JV, sets the two-year rule, requires a written JV with its own name identified in SAM, bars populated JVs on set-asides unless all partners are similarly situated, and states the ostensible subcontractor rule. Paragraph (b) holds the exceptions (mentor-protégé, Small Business Teaming Arrangements); (f) identity of interest; (g) newly organized concern.
key_facts: (h): a JV is an association "intending to engage in and carry out business ventures for joint profit over a two-year period".

Two-year rule: a specific JV generally may not be awarded contracts beyond two years from the date of award of its first contract; after that the partners are deemed affiliated for new offers. An offer submitted before the two years end may be awarded afterwards. The same partners may form a new JV with its own two-year period. Orders under a previously awarded contract may be issued beyond the two years.
(h)(1): JV must be in writing, do business under its own name, and be identified as a JV in SAM; may be a formal or informal partnership or a separate legal entity.

(h)(1): a separate-legal-entity JV cannot be populated with individuals intended to perform set-aside contracts unless all parties are similarly situated; it may have its own employees for administrative functions, including Facility Security Officer(s).

(h)(2): a JV may submit an offer as small if each concern is small under the NAICS size standard; a mentor-protégé JV under 125.9 is small if the protégé is small and the JV meets 124.513(c)-(d), 125.8(b)-(c), 126.616(c)-(d), 127.506(c)-(d) or 128.402(c)-(d) as applicable.

(h)(3): ostensible subcontractor — a subcontractor that is not similarly situated and performs the primary and vital requirements, or on which the prime is unusually reliant, makes the offeror ineligible as small. General construction: primary and vital = management, supervision and oversight, not the construction work itself. Services/specialty trade/supplies: prime meets the test if, with similarly situated subs, it meets 125.6.
(h)(4): each partner counts its proportionate share of JV receipts (same percentage as its share of work; ownership percentage for populated JVs) and employees.

(f): identity of interest — family members presumed affiliated if they do business with each other; economic dependence presumed where a concern derived 70% or more of receipts from another concern over the previous three fiscal years; both rebuttable.
(b)(6): a firm with an SBA-approved mentor-protégé agreement is not affiliated with its mentor or protégé solely because the protégé receives assistance under the agreement.

(b)(9): for bundled or multiple-award contracts above the substantial bundling threshold, a small prime may team with small subcontractors under a Small Business Teaming Arrangement without affiliation if each member is small.
(g): newly organized concern rule — former officers/key employees starting a firm in the same or related industry with assistance from the old firm; rebuttable by a clear line of fracture.
(h)(3): ostensible subcontractor is one that is not a similarly situated entity and performs primary and vital requirements, or on which the prime is unusually reliant.
For services and specialty trade construction, a prime meets the test if it and small-business subs together meet the 125.6 limitations on subcontracting.
(h): a specific joint venture generally may not be awarded contracts beyond two years from the first award without the partners being deemed affiliated.
(f)(2): presumption of affiliation where a concern derived 70% or more of its receipts from another concern over the previous three fiscal years; rebuttable.
(h)(2): SBA-approved mentor and protégé may joint venture as small if the protégé is small for the NAICS code.

date_note: Sweep gave published: up to date as of 10/01/2026; last amendment 89 FR 102492 (Dec. 17, 2024)
summary: The program rule. Any for-profit firm of any size may mentor; a protégé must be small in its primary NAICS code or an identified secondary code where it has experience. An approved agreement lets mentor and protégé joint venture as small for any contract the protégé is small for, and lets the mentor hold up to 40% of the protégé.
key_facts: (b): mentor is a for-profit concern of any size with good character and a favourable financial position, not debarred or suspended.

(b)(3): a mentor (with parent and subsidiaries in aggregate) generally cannot have more than three protégés at one time; the first two relationships with Puerto Rico-based small businesses do not count; a mentor that buys another mentor may carry that firm's protégés in addition.
(b)(3)(i): a mentor with more than one protégé cannot submit competing offers on the same procurement through separate JVs.
(b)(4): a mentor cannot be a contract holder through JVs with two protégés on the same small-business multiple-award contract.
(c)(1): protégé qualifies as small for its primary NAICS code, or a secondary code in which it has prior experience.
(c)(2): generally one mentor at a time; SBA may approve a second where it will not compete or conflict.
(c)(4): generally a total of two mentor-protégé agreements with different mentors; a concern cannot be a protégé for more than 12 years in total.

(d)(1): a protégé-mentor JV is small for any procurement for which the protégé individually is small; SBA must approve the mentor-protégé agreement before the JV submits an offer; once the protégé is no longer small for the contract's NAICS code the JV cannot recertify as small; protégé has a right of first refusal on the mentor's JV interest.
(d)(1)(iii): a change in the protégé's size does not generally affect contracts already awarded to the JV.
(d)(2): mentor may own up to 40% of the protégé.
(d)(4): no affiliation or control found solely on the basis of the agreement.

(e): written agreement with needs assessment, assistance and timeline, single point of contact; mentor commits for at least one year; either party may terminate on 30 days' notice; term may not exceed six years; shorter agreements may be extended up to six years from inception; SBA must approve changes.
(f): if SBA declines, the firm may not reapply with the same mentor for 60 calendar days.

(g): protégé reports within 30 days of each anniversary: assistance received, loans/equity, subcontracts, JV contracts, narrative; services reported by category and hours; annual certification of any change in terms. SBA may decline continuation where assistance was not provided or yielded no material benefit.

(h): mentor has 30 days to respond to a finding of non-performance; SBA terminates the agreement, bars the firm as a mentor for two years, may recommend stop-work orders on JV contracts, and may treat it as grounds for debarment.
(i): protégé reports at the end whether the relationship was beneficial.
quotes: A joint venture between a protégé and its mentor will qualify as a small business for any procurement for which the protégé individually qualifies as …
The term of a mentor-protégé agreement may not exceed six years.
The protégé firm may agree to sell or otherwise convey to the mentor an equity interest of up to 40% in the protégé firm.
